note: One strong reading per PPDT picture (D33), shown after the candidate's own attempt. Each has a hero near the candidate's age, a realistic problem, positive action and an outcome: past, present, future. Not the answer: one way among many.

samples.ppdt-01: Kunal, a 20-year-old engineering student, was waiting on platform 1 for the 12:50 train home. He saw a man on crutches making for the coach while an older woman, his mother, watched anxiously beside their bags. With two minutes left, Kunal asked a fellow traveller to keep an eye on the luggage, helped the man up the steps and lifted the bags in after him. On the journey he learnt the man had lost his leg in a flood rescue. Moved by the story, Kunal joined the NCC that term and later went on to train as a disaster-relief volunteer in his district.
samples.ppdt-02: Naik Dorje, 24, was leading a four-man patrol across a rock face to reach a stranded survey team before nightfall. A loose ledge had cut off the usual path, so he roped the team together and chose a longer line across firmer rock. When the last man slipped, Dorje anchored the rope and held him until the others pulled him up. They reached the surveyors by dusk, shared their rations and guided them down the next morning. The company commander later used Dorje's route to mark a safer track for every patrol that followed.
samples.ppdt-03: Mr Tandon, a young teacher at a hill school, noticed that half his class of sixteen-year-olds were failing mathematics because they feared it. One morning he stopped the lesson, put away the textbook and asked each student to bring a problem from home: the price of vegetables, the bus fare, their fathers' crop loans. For a month he taught every topic through those problems, and the students began to argue answers among themselves. He set up evening groups led by the stronger students. At the board examination the whole class passed, and the next year the school adopted his method for every section.
samples.ppdt-04: Rohan, a 23-year-old junior engineer, had found a calculation error in a bridge design due for approval that week. At the review he stood and pressed the point hard, while a senior colleague argued from his chair that the schedule could not slip. The project head smiled and asked Rohan to show his numbers. He walked them through the loads step by step until the error was plain to all. The design went back for a fortnight's rework, and the bridge later opened safely. Rohan was asked to check every design that came after.
samples.ppdt-05: Dr Varsha, a 26-year-old doctor on her first posting, ran a health camp in a village where a fever had spread for two weeks. With the senior doctor at the microscope and a volunteer, Gopal, keeping the queue, she tested every patient's blood and found malaria in most. She asked the village elders to gather the men the same evening and explained how still water in the old tank was breeding mosquitoes. Next morning the young men drained the tank while she treated the sick and gave out nets. Within three weeks the fever had gone, and the district later held the same camp in ten villages.
samples.ppdt-06: Raghav, 21, had queued at the Employment Exchange for the third time that month, along with friends who had studied with him. He noticed that most of the men in the queue had trade skills but no certificates. Instead of waiting, he asked the officer which courses the nearby industrial training institute ran and what the factories needed. He gathered six of the young men, enrolled them in a three-month welding course and arranged a room where they practised every evening. All six passed, and within a month of the course four of them, Raghav among them, had found jobs at the new steel plant.
samples.ppdt-07: Neha, 22, had stayed up past midnight finishing a project report due at nine the next morning. Tired and stuck on the final section, she rested her head in her hand and felt like giving up. Then she remembered her mentor's advice to break a big task into small steps. She listed what remained, finished the charts first and wrote the conclusion in short points. By two she had a complete draft and slept for four hours. Her presentation the next day went well, and the company later offered her a place on the project team.
samples.ppdt-08: Kavita, a 26-year-old teacher, received a letter from home saying her father had fallen ill and the harvest was due in a week. Worried, she read it twice, then sat down to plan. She spoke to her headmistress, who arranged for a colleague to take her classes for ten days. She called her cousin, a nurse, to visit her father the same evening, and booked the morning bus. At home she organised the harvest with the neighbours' help while her father recovered. She returned to school on time, and later set up a phone tree for the village's elderly.
samples.ppdt-09: Rekha, a 24-year-old nurse on the night shift, was taking a patient back from the operation theatre when she saw his younger brother following the trolley, silent and frightened. The operation had been long, and the man had not eaten all day. Rekha settled the patient in the ward, checked his drip and then sat the brother down and explained, step by step, what the surgeon had done and what the night would bring. She brought him tea and showed him where to rest. By morning the patient was awake and talking. The family later thanked the hospital, and Rekha was asked to train new nurses in caring for relatives.
samples.ppdt-10: Aditya, 19, found his younger sister crying in the college garden after her result showed she had failed one paper. She felt she had let the family down and wanted to drop out. Aditya wiped her tears, sat her on a bench and asked her to show him the paper. Together they saw she had lost marks for leaving questions half done, not for not knowing. He made her a timetable, practised timed papers with her every evening and asked her teacher for the old question papers. At the supplementary examination she passed with good marks, and she went on to finish the course in the first division.
samples.ppdt-11: Kabir, 20, was on a college trip to the beach when he saw a small boy wading out alone towards a strong current while the families around were busy with their picnic. He ran into the water, caught the boy before the waves turned and carried him back to shore. The boy's parents had been searching for him by the van. Kabir then spoke to the lifeguard about a flag for the dangerous stretch, and with his friends he roped it off for the rest of the day. The next season the municipality put up warning boards and a lifeguard tower at that very spot.
samples.ppdt-12: Sahil, 22, was crossing the market when a man snatched a gold chain from a woman in a cycle-rickshaw and ran. As she cried out, Sahil shouted to two young men nearby to block the lane ahead and sprinted after the thief himself. The man turned into a side street, but the other two were waiting there, and together they held him until the beat constable arrived. Sahil returned the chain to the woman and gave his statement at the police station. The thief was found to be part of a gang, and the police later caught three more of its members.
samples.ppdt-13: Nikhil, 20, was trekking home from college when he found the rope bridge to his village broken, its planks lying on the bank after a flood. The river was too fast to wade, and the village school children crossed this way every day. He walked an hour to the next village, phoned the block office and then gathered the young men of his village that evening. They collected the planks, borrowed rope and tools from the forest office and, with a carpenter's help, rebuilt the bridge in four days. Since then the young men check it after every monsoon.
samples.ppdt-14: Four friends from the same college, led by Ankita, had built a small model of a low-cost water filter for the state science fair. The night before, the base cracked and the filter stopped working. Ankita gathered the team round the table and asked each one to list what could have gone wrong. They found the clay base had dried too fast. Working through the night, they rebuilt it with a cement layer and tested it three times. At the fair the judges praised the design, the team won second prize, and a local panchayat later asked them to build filters for its school.
samples.ppdt-15: Omkar, 17, was preparing for his board examinations while also helping his father at the shop every evening. With a month left, he found he was behind in physics. He made a timetable that used every early morning, asked his teacher for extra problems and studied at his desk from five till school. When his father fell ill, he took the shop's accounts to his desk and did them between chapters. He finished the syllabus a week before the examination and revised it twice. He scored ninety-two in physics, and his teacher later asked him to coach the juniors.
samples.ppdt-16: Pradeep, a 25-year-old agriculture graduate, came back to his village and saw the farmers losing half their crop each year to waterlogging. He called the men under the banyan tree and explained, with a drawing in the dust, how raised beds and a drainage channel would save the crop. The elders doubted him, so he offered to try it first on his own family's field. That season his field gave twice the yield of the others. The next year twenty farmers followed him, and the agriculture department later invited him to teach the method in the block.
samples.ppdt-17: Vikram, 23, a forest guard, was crossing the rope bridge over the gorge to reach a remote hamlet where a child was reported ill and the road had been cut by a landslide. Halfway over he saw that two planks had worked loose. He tied them down with his belt and spare rope so the bridge would hold, crossed safely and carried the medicines to the hamlet. He waited until the doctor arrived by the same bridge. Back at his post he reported the damage, and within a week the forest department had the bridge repaired and the planks replaced.
samples.ppdt-18: Amit, 24, an agriculture officer on his first posting, visited a farmer whose wheat yield had fallen three years in a row. Walking the field with him, Amit found the soil short of nutrients from years of the same crop. He explained crop rotation and a soil test, and offered to arrange both free under a government scheme. The farmer laughed at first but agreed to try on one plot. Amit returned every fortnight to check the plot. At harvest that plot gave forty per cent more, and the farmer later persuaded his neighbours to sign up for the scheme.
samples.ppdt-19: Manoj, 19, was walking home from college when a car hit a scooter at the crossing and the young rider fell under it. People gathered, but no one moved. Manoj asked the driver to stay where he was, asked two men to keep the traffic back and checked the rider's breathing. He called the ambulance, and with the others lifted the car's edge carefully while a shopkeeper eased the rider out. He pressed his handkerchief on the bleeding until the ambulance came and went with him to the hospital. The rider recovered, and his family thanked Manoj at the police station.
samples.ppdt-20: Suresh, 28, had just been told his small printing business would have to close after he lost his biggest order. He sat alone in the empty office, head in his hands, wondering how he would pay his two workers. After an hour he stood up, took a sheet of paper and listed every school, office and shop within five kilometres. Over the next week he visited each one with samples and offered fast delivery at fair rates. Twelve small orders came in, enough to keep the press running. Within six months the business had recovered, and he later took on a third worker.
samples.ppdt-21: Deepak, 21, the student union secretary, learnt that the college was to close its library in the evenings because of a shortage of staff, just before the examinations. Students gathered outside the office shouting, and some wanted a strike. Deepak raised his hand to quiet them and proposed a better way: student volunteers would run the issue counter in the evenings. He took the plan and twenty volunteers' names to the principal the same day. The principal agreed to a trial. The library stayed open till nine, results improved that year, and the scheme has run ever since.
